strengths: The integration of label propagation and label spreading into BORE is coherent and potentially useful. It exploits candidate geometry without additional objective evaluations and accommodates both sampled unlabeled points and predefined pools. This combination can constitute a contribution despite using established components.

The experiments cover synthetic optimization, tabular hyperparameter optimization, NATS-Bench, and an image-based search task, with 20 seeded repetitions and standard errors. Figures 2 and 6 show substantial improvements over several relevant baselines, particularly on continuous synthetic functions and NATS-Bench.

The manuscript explains its relationship to BORE and LFBO, provides algorithmic descriptions and an inductive prediction rule, and investigates bandwidth, sampling distributions, unlabeled sample counts, pool subsampling, and threshold ratios.
weaknesses: The central benefit of unlabeled data is insufficiently isolated. Figure 12 includes a useful no-transduction kernel baseline, but fixes beta at 0.5, whereas the headline experiments learn beta at every iteration. The baseline is competitive or superior in several of these ablations. Comparisons using the same bandwidth-selection procedure and acquisition optimization are needed to distinguish the contribution of semi-supervised learning from kernel smoothing and tuning. The random tie-breaking heuristic also needs an ablation, alongside simple random-search and exploration-enhanced supervised-classifier controls.

The proposed explanation for improved exploration remains heuristic. Sampling truncated Gaussians around evaluated points does not ensure that high-density connected regions share the same threshold label, especially as the threshold changes. Appendix C acknowledges that the cited independent-sampling guarantees do not apply to sequential optimization, and does not establish the claimed beneficial expansion of the positive decision region. The qualitative Branin illustrations therefore provide limited support for the general claim of resolving over-exploitation.

Important reproduction details remain unspecified: input normalization, the label-spreading clamping factor and stopping settings, bandwidth optimization initialization and bounds, and acquisition maximization over finite pools. Baseline acquisition-optimization procedures are also unclear. These choices materially affect graph distances and comparison quality. A smaller mathematical correction is needed in Section 4.1: the column-normalized definition of p_ij is inconsistent with the stated matrix expression P = D^{-1}W.

The scope of the evidence is narrower than the broad performance claims suggest. All continuous benchmarks are two-dimensional, and the tabular results are mixed. The 64-dimensional MNIST experiment uses representations trained with the same digit-value labels that define the optimization objective. Although shared representations permit a valid comparison, this substantial task supervision limits the experiment's support for general high-dimensional black-box optimization; ranking candidates with the pretrained classifier would be an informative control.

Practical computational performance is incompletely evaluated. Dense graph construction, repeated propagation during bandwidth optimization, and 1,000 acquisition restarts can be expensive. Figure 14 studies subset-size scaling with fixed beta, but provides neither comparative runtime against the baselines nor the overhead of the complete headline procedure.
